title: The six-agent pitch
scenario: A software vendor pitches an agent system to your studio for 30-second ads. You judge its limits before anyone signs. The pitch, the numbers and the notes are made up for this case. The vendor lines are copied from the docs.
exhibit:
PROPOSAL FROM A SOFTWARE VENDOR (made up for this case)
  "Autopilot Studio": six agents, one per step.
    1 concept  2 storyboard  3 image  4 video  5 voice  6 review
  Credentials: the brand's admin login for the social account, so any agent
               can fix anything it finds.
  First run:   straight on the client's live account.

CHAIN MATHS (made up for this case)
  The chain has 5 steps. Each step is right 90 times out of 100.

CAMPAIGN NOTES (made up for this case)
  The agent runs on a Google managed agent (Public Preview). Last Monday it
  paused to wait for the client's reply. The reply came 10 days later.

VENDOR LINES (copied from the docs)
  OpenAI: "Start with one agent whenever you can."
  Google: "The agent may use any credential it has access to, so only provide
          credentials whose full scope you are willing to grant."
  Google: "Environments are permanently deleted after 7 days of inactivity."
  Anthropic: "We recommend extensive testing in sandboxed environments, along
          with the appropriate guardrails."

questions.prompt: About how often will all 5 steps be right, using the numbers in the exhibit?

options.text: About 90 times out of 100, because each single step is right 90 times out of 100
options.explanation: The chance that all steps are right is lower than the chance of one step. Errors add up along a chain.

options.text: About 50 times out of 100, because with five steps the chances are cut exactly in half
options.explanation: There is no rule that halves the chance. Multiply 0.9 five times.

options.text: About 59 times out of 100, which is the number 0.9 multiplied by itself five times
options.explanation: Right. 0.9 x 0.9 x 0.9 x 0.9 x 0.9 is about 0.59. Anthropic warns of compounding errors. The numbers are made up for this case.

options.text: About 95 times out of 100, because the review step catches almost every earlier mistake
options.explanation: A review step helps, but it is one more step with its own chance of error, and it does not make the chain safe.

questions.prompt: What do you advise about the six-agent plan?

options.text: Start with one agent and its tools, and add a specialist only for a clear reason
options.explanation: Right. OpenAI says to start with one agent and add specialists only when they materially improve isolation, clarity or traces.

options.text: Accept all six, because one agent per step is the cleanest design for any creative chain
options.explanation: OpenAI warns that splitting too early creates more prompts, traces and approval surfaces.

options.text: Use twelve agents instead, two for each step, so that every step is double-checked
options.explanation: More agents add more prompts and traces. The guide says to add specialists only when needed.

options.text: Use one agent with no tools at all, so that nothing can go wrong during the run
options.explanation: An agent with no tools cannot make media. The advice is to start simple, not to remove its tools.

questions.prompt: The vendor wants to give the agents the brand's admin login. What is the better choice?

options.text: Give the admin login, because a stronger login means fewer errors and fewer pauses for approval
options.explanation: A stronger login means a bigger mistake if the agent is wrong.

options.text: Give a key that can do only what the job needs, such as saving drafts, and nothing else
options.explanation: Right. Google says to provide only credentials whose full scope you are willing to grant, and advises least privilege.

options.text: Give the admin login but hide it, so that the agent cannot use it unless it truly needs it
options.explanation: Google says the agent may use any credential it can access. Hiding it from the prompt is not a limit.

options.text: Give the login of an intern, because an intern's account is always small and is safe to use
options.explanation: An account's size is not its scope. Choose the narrowest access for the task, not a person's login.

questions.prompt: The client's reply came after 10 days. What is the risk, and what should the studio have done?

options.text: There is no risk, because an agent keeps its workspace for ever once a job has started
options.explanation: Google gives a 7-day limit for inactive environments.

options.text: The risk is only that the agent forgets the client's name, which a short note can fix
options.explanation: The risk is the loss of the whole environment, including files.

options.text: The client's reply is too late to use, so the studio should never wait for any reply
options.explanation: Waiting is normal. The design should survive a wait, by keeping copies outside the agent.

options.text: The 7-day limit may have deleted the environment, so keep your own copies outside it
options.explanation: Right. Google says environments are permanently deleted after 7 days of inactivity. This is a Public Preview feature.

questions.prompt: The vendor plans to run the first job on the client's live account. What do you say?

options.text: Fine, because the agent has been tested by the vendor on its own demo brands
options.explanation: A vendor's demo does not test this studio's accounts, tools or rubric.

options.text: Fine, as long as the agent writes a note about each action it takes on the live account
options.explanation: A note after the action does not undo it. Test first, where a mistake does no harm.

options.text: Run the first jobs in a sandbox, on a dummy brand, with a test account and no posting
options.explanation: Right. Anthropic recommends extensive testing in sandboxed environments, along with guardrails.

options.text: Fine, since the approval card will catch every problem before it reaches the public
options.explanation: An approval helps, but a first run should still be tested where a mistake does no harm.
